title: Chirality-resolved imaging of spin waves with a quantum spin
authors: Enbo Zhang, Tiancheng Zheng, Bo-Yuan Yang, Shreyes Nallan, Chengchao Xu, Mark Ku, Jian-Gang Zhu
abstract: Spin waves carry their propagation direction in the handedness of their circularly polarized stray field, a property inaccessible to scalar magnetometers. In the Damon-Eshbach surface wave of an in-plane magnetized film, the dipolar field above the film rotates with a handedness fixed by the direction of travel. The nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centre in diamond is an intrinsic polarization analyser: a right-handed field about the NV axis drives one spin transition, and a left-handed field drives the other, in both the ground and the excited state. Here, we exploit the two excited-state transitions, which lie inside the spin-wave band of yttrium iron garnet (YIG), as a pair of chirality channels and image Damon-Eshbach waves in both directions. Because reflection from an etched boundary reverses the handedness, the incident and reflected waves appear as two lines in one spectrum and are imaged separately. In the ground state, the same rule applies, and the selected field drives Rabi oscillations, a route to chirality-selective control of the NV spin by magnons. Reading the two channels gives the direction of a spin wave at one point, without a phase reference. This advances chirality-resolved quantum sensing and provides insight into chiral spin-wave dynamics.
summary: This research demonstrates a novel technique to image the chirality of spin waves using Nitrogen-Vacancy (NV) centers as intrinsic polarization analyzers. By exploiting the NV center's sensitivity to circularly polarized magnetic fields, the authors successfully distinguish between wave propagation directions and even detect the reversal of chirality upon reflection. This advances quantum sensing by providing a phase-reference-free method for characterizing chiral spin-wave dynamics.
main_problem: The primary goal is to develop a method to directly image the chirality (handedness) of propagating spin waves, a property inaccessible to conventional scalar magnetometers.
main_result: The Nitrogen-Vacancy (NV) center successfully images Damon-Eshbach waves in both propagation directions, and critically, it demonstrates that reflection reverses the wave's chirality, allowing for unambiguous direction sensing.
method: The study uses Optically Detected Magnetic Resonance (ODMR) scanning single-NV magnetometry above a YIG thin film to exploit the NV center's intrinsic polarization analysis capability.
model_or_system: The system involves spin waves (Damon-Eshbach surface waves) propagating in an in-plane magnetized YIG film, detected by the NV center in diamond. The NV center acts as a chiral analyzer because its transitions are sensitive to the circular polarization ($\sigma+$ vs. $\sigma-$) of the local stray magnetic field.
key_observables: Chirality contrast ratio ($\sigma+$ vs. $\sigma-$), decay lengths ($L$), and the separation of incident and reflected wave components in distinct chiral channels.
important_parameters: Bias field strength (e.g., $\pm 6$ mT), frequency (e.g., 1.53 and 1.31 GHz), and the geometry of the etched boundaries (pits/trenches).
main_assumptions: The method relies fundamentally on the NV center's ability to resolve circular polarization and the assumption that the spin wave dynamics are governed by established micromagnetic models.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the NV center's role as a chirality analyzer, showing how chirality follows $	ext{sgn}(k_x) \cdot 	ext{sgn}(z)$. They demonstrate channel swapping upon field reversal and the clean separation of incident and reflected waves into distinct chiral channels.
paper_structure: The paper logically establishes the need for chirality detection, details the NV center's mechanism as a chiral analyzer, and then presents experimental evidence through various geometries (striplines, etched pits, reflectors) to confirm chirality-resolved imaging and directionality.
why_interesting: This work provides a highly sensitive, non-contact quantum sensing platform for characterizing fundamental wave properties (chirality) in condensed matter systems, bridging quantum sensing with classical magnetism.
